biography.plain_text: Nick Robertson is a British entrepreneur who co-founded ASOS, the online fashion retailer, after working in advertising and establishing a marketing agency. His brother Nigel supplied half the business's original funding. Robertson led ASOS as chief executive until 2015, remained on its board and became chair of the ASOS Foundation.

long_biography.plain_text:
Retail entrepreneur Nick Robertson recruited former Topshop buyer Lorri Penn when ASOS still sold a mixture of products associated with television and film. Her clothing selections drew the strongest response, prompting him to concentrate the business on fashion. He nevertheless favoured selling other brands alongside the higher-margin own-label range, rather than making the website a single-brand shop.

In Wimbledon, he bought newly issued shares in the local football club's holding company to help close the funding gap for its new stadium. His equity investment supplied construction capital without adding interest payments, while the supporters' Dons Trust retained control.

uncertainties: Current industry is explicitly a fallback. The known retained listed stake and other investments are not a comprehensive personal portfolio, and the historical sale proceeds cannot be assumed to remain in any particular sector.

Retained meaningful ownership plus current governance supports Founder at medium confidence. This does not assert executive control, majority share ownership or that every current asset belongs to ASOS. Investor was independently tested against private allocations.
Substantial brother-supplied startup investment establishes an advantaged separate build. An ancestry link to Austin Reed is unnecessary to that inference and is not treated as inherited ownership.
The later fashion investment's administration is business-specific. Historical roles remain dated; neither personal bankruptcy nor complete loss of the founder's other capital is inferred.

Audited holdings include Person Closely Associated interests. The entry is reported under Robertson; no exact beneficial split among associated persons is supplied, and no individual current net-worth number is imported.

No exact birth day, town or country found at sufficient confidence. Surrey upbringing and a UK school are not proof of birthplace. Nationality and ordinary residence are already supported in the immutable record.
Forbes-first dedicated-profile search completed without a match. Articles on the retailer and sports namesakes are not Forbes personal profiles.

All supported personal types checked: Instagram, Personal Website, Facebook, Twitter/X, Youtube, TikTok, Vimeo, Flickr, Trip Advisor and Zillow, together with existing LinkedIn/Wikipedia and Company Website. No new authenticated personal account identified. Corporate accounts, interview channels and namesake accounts are excluded.
Existing LinkedIn direct access was blocked; matching business-directory context is not treated as a fresh personal-account verification. Existing links are retained without duplicate additions.

Family support, asset materiality and current role were judged separately. The company Foundation's assets are not counted as personal property. The stadium investment is personal equity, not a charitable gift or sole funding of the entire project.

Single-source budgets include repeated brief and metadata derivation. The 2010 sale report contributes fewer than25 derived words; ASOS report economic details and biography facts are kept compact. No court-related private-family detail is used.
